quoted_tweet.text:
Black & Scholes gives risk-neutral option prices.

The expected return of the underlying is irrelevant as it's hedged away to create an arbitrage-free price.

However, if you trade an option without hedging, then the expected return certainly does matter. How can you reconcile this with the option prices you're quoted?

You can modify Black & Scholes to accept a drift parameter. Sinclair explains this in Positional Option Trading. This adjusted formula lets you translate a directional view into a subjective option price.

Here's a tool that implements it:
https://t.co/xaHG8kpix5

You can input an estimated forward price for a given expiration. Drift gets inferred from that.

You can also input a variance risk premium to account for the drag of IV potentially being overstated.

You'll find that, in absolute terms, ITM/ATM strikes get more lift from a higher forward whereas OTM strikes tend to get a larger relative multiplier.

quoted_tweet.text:
Continuing the short straddle backtest.

Let's add a delta-hedge each day at 8am utc.

What happens?

The infamous 1st week of Feb doesn't look as scary anymore. The stand-alone hedging P&L was strong that week.

How did that work:
• Underlying price crashed
• Short put started to dominate
• Short straddle went increasingly long delta
• Delta-hedger was simply shorting the trend

The trend was your friend.

One of the worst weeks was when the straddle broke even.

How did that play out:
• Sold 102k strike with BTC ~101k
• Mid-week it went up to 106k
• Our hedge was to be long delta
• Then price crashed to 96k into expiry

You don't want price to blow through the strike into expiration.

Overall, you clearly see the mechanics of hedging in the chart.

Hedging a short straddle means replicating a long straddle in the underlying. Your hedging becomes trend-following. You buy delta as price goes up, you sell delta as price goes down.

The replication payoff is negatively correlated to the payoff of the short straddle so the net effect is lower variance and reduced max drawdown.

Our futures rolls are structurally difficult to price.

MMs need to do multiple things at once:

• But also forecast funding rates on thalex
• Then assess funding rate gamma by expiry 
• And somehow fit a consistent term structure

Over the last few days, Thalex went from suppressed to  normalized funding. It's hard to predict these regime shifts. Mainly MMs adapt in response to trades telling them they need to price basis higher.

Smart retail has the taker edge.

They can hide in the tall grass, look for bumps in term structure, compare thalex roll prices to deribit ... then pull the trigger whenever they see a big divergence.

quoted_tweet.text:
How to buy the dip with calls?

Notes from last night, as I tried not to overthink it.

First, maturity selection.

Two general ideas:

(1) Maturity should be decided based on exposure rather than the time horizon of the trade. At the core, this is about deciding whether you want gamma or vega.

(2) Options expiring in <1 week are brutally hard. They tend to be optically cheap but very expensive in vol-terms, suffer from wild delta and vol swings and they decay very fast.

I'd lean towards 1-3 months to expiry to get a more stable delta exposure and better ratio of delta/theta. I'd only look at shorter maturities if gamma looks very cheap.

Yesterday:

As btc broke 80k, IVs jumped to 50-60% for next week, hence gamma quickly got repriced. The cheapest expiries were 27-Feb/Mar (44-45%).

Then it becomes about theta vs premium. Theta decay  non-linearly increases towards expiration. A longer expiration time window gives more breathing room on theta: $50/day for 27-Mar (atm θ) compared to $70 for 27-Feb, despite option premia for Mar being higher.

March it is then.

Second, strike selection.

This is ultimately about having a directional view.

Make this as sophisticated as you like: technical analysis, order flow (h/t @MMT_Official_)... Do whatever works for you and import experience from perps.

My take yesterday:

When you lose a key range with large liquidations, there is a spike in realize vol. High RV is sticky short-term. Altogether, good odds of an upper retest. 80K sits nicely under key levels on high time frames for the range we just lost. I reckon $1-2K upside on a $4k premium.

And that's about it, really.

A decision made in <60 seconds.

Below you see it playing out.

Notice how the P&L is primarily delta, while net gamma vs theta is insignificant.

Vega is a detractor, which is usually the case if you buy the dip because of the price down, vol up <> price up, vol down pattern we observe ever since ETFs launched. 

The vega risk is contained in my view. What is the chance of IV dropping to for instance, <40 IV, given that we just entered a price range not seen since Apr'25?

Final note - delta is king:

Time the entry based on underlying price.

The P&L composition illustrates this. The 80k 27-Mar call has ~$120 vega, so a 1% vol difference is 4x less important than a $1k better entry on price for an atm option, especially for longer expiries where IV usually doesn't reprice as sharply.

quoted_tweet.text:
If you sell a future against a perp, you have a delta-neutral trade that depends heavily on the index price.

Contradiction?

Let's take an extreme example. You sold futures at 120k spot, 8% annual basis, and entered a long perp to hedge.

When you sold that future, you locked in basis as an absolute dollar-amount of ~$4k using a March future.

Then the index price went down. 

The perp leg got charged funding rate * index progressively. Even if the funding rate were constant at 8% annual as well, the index price on which it applies averaged down, so you still get + carry.

Then there is correlation between price and carry. As price goes down, rates compress.

Basis went from 8% to 0% and funding rates went down as well. That's an additional directional lever. Basis gets marked lower (+ pnl) and funding cost decreases (also + pnl).

So futures spreads are quite directionally levered through (1) debasement and (2) re-rating.

Delta-neutral delta.

That's what makes these interesting to trade in my opinion.

quoted_tweet.text:
Option implied probabilities are kind of ‘dumb’.

Or better said, intelligent in a narrow sense.

Market makers fit option prices to a volatility surface. Their main goal is internal consistency: prices across strikes and expiries must be coherent so they cannot be mechanically arbitraged.

Those prices imply a risk-neutral distribution whose mean is the forward price. Under no-arbitrage pricing that forward reflects carry, not expected returns. Market makers delta hedge, they don’t need to forecast spot to price options.

So the distribution implied by options is not meant to predict the possible paths of spot. It is not a “real-world” distribution but a pricing device that keeps quotes arbitrage-free.

That is why it can miss context a discretionary trader sees: a level of support that is held, momentum building, which range high is likely to be retested. Options prices only adapt to these dynamics when positional traders lift orders.

Hence, you should feel free to disagree with implied probabilities.

For example, the BTC 27-Mar 80k call has a 9 % risk-neutral probability of expiring in the money. Say you assign a 60 % chance of moving up, and conditional on moving up you give a ⅓ chance of finishing above 80k. Your subjective probability is 20 %, and you see value in buying the call.

quoted_tweet.text:
I'm not smart enough to trade calendar spreads.

They sound like a good idea when volatility term structure gets inverted: "Sell expensive IV in the front, buy cheap IV in the back."

But that's not the exposure you get with a calendar.

Let's look at an example from the fast market on Feb 5th. Say that, with btc at 60k, you sold the 20-Feb 60k call and bought the 27-Mar 60k call.

You sold a call for ~90% IV and bought a call for ~70% IV.

Why is this a losing trade?

Delta
The Feb call is relatively more sensitive to a change in underlying price. The calendar was initially ± Δ-neutral, but as the market recovered, the Δ of the call in Feb went up more than the call in Mar, so you picked up a short delta position.

Vega
Options with longer maturities have more vega. This makes the calendar net long vega. In essence, you're long forward vol between Feb and Mar. How could you expect to make money on that if you locked in Mar vol at 70?

As IV shifted down in parallel across the term structure, the vega P&L started bleeding.

quoted_tweet.text:
The options market is the biggest in terms of leverage efficiency.

Because of this, they have a huge impact on the whole market.
